explanations: luna: The section's dictionary form خَلِيقَة names a rock hollow collecting rain; here water bursts from a struck rock into twelve springs, and each group عَلِمَ its drinking place. The ayah gives both a rock-water scene and the source section's علم family beside an assigned water source. | terra: A struck stone releases twelve springs and each people عَلِمَ its drinking place; this meets both the source dictionary's water-holding rock hollow and its ʿ-l-m family image of a water-rich well.

luna: The section's dictionary entry describes water collected in hollows in rock; this ayah says some stones split and water comes out. The direction differs, but it makes the rock itself a source or vessel for water. | terra: Rocks here gush rivers or split so water comes out, reversing the dictionary image in which a hollow in rock receives and holds water from heaven.
terra: The same ayah names ships running بِمَا يَنفَعُ ٱلنَّاسَ and water sent from heaven to revive earth, joining the section's root of benefit to beneficial rain.
terra: Wine and gambling contain مَنَافِعُ, yet their sin is greater than their benefit; this qualifies the source definition by showing that an isolated benefit need not lead to good.
luna: The section contrasts waste with what benefits and remains; this ayah likens charitable giving to a grain that multiplies into many ears. It shows useful growth producing a lasting return.

luna: The section makes a reminder conditional on benefit; this ayah describes giving without following it with reminders of favor or injury, and promises reward. It brings speech and beneficial giving into the same moral scene.

luna: The section asks whether a reminder benefits; this ayah says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. It gives a specific verbal good that outlasts a show of material giving.

luna: The section distinguishes useful water from what a torrent carries off; this ayah's rain strikes a thinly covered rock and leaves it bare, as a picture of deeds that yield nothing. It makes the loss of apparent benefit concrete. | terra: A downpour strips soil from a smooth rock and leaves it bare, so ostentatious spending yields nothing; this reverses the source image of a rock hollow retaining beneficial rain.

luna: The section's rock hollows gather rainwater for growth; this ayah pictures a garden on high ground receiving heavy rain or drizzle and yielding double. It is the fruitful counterpart to 2:264's rain-washed bare rock. | terra: A well-placed garden gives doubled produce under a downpour and still yields under drizzle, making retained rain an image of expenditure that truly benefits.

luna: The section contrasts useful growth with what is swept away; this ayah pictures a garden with rivers destroyed by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and dependent. It makes the loss of accumulated yield especially concrete.
terra: Gold, silver, and other desired goods are named as worldly adornment and temporary enjoyment; these are the ornaments for which 13:17's metals are worked, now placed on the passing side.

luna: The section's pasture becomes debris and its proverb names what is lost; this ayah compares unproductive spending to a freezing wind that destroys a people's crop. It gives another specific image of weather carrying away a hoped-for yield. | terra: A freezing wind destroys the crop of people who wrong themselves, reversing the beneficial rain-and-growth sequence and leaving effort without useful yield.
terra: Worldly enjoyment is called little and the hereafter خَيْرٌ for the God-fearing, a concise parallel to the section's better-and-lasting judgment.
terra: God يَعْلَمُ both سِرَّكُمْ and جَهْرَكُمْ; the roots of “knows” and “manifest” meet in the same open/hidden relation from which the section derives its well image.
terra: Worldly life is play and diversion while the hereafter's abode is better for the God-fearing, a repeated formulation of 87:16–17's choice.

luna: The section connects cloud water with pasture; this ayah sends down water and brings out varied crops, palms, gardens, and fruit. It supplies a distinct formulation of rain producing useful growth. | terra: Heavenly water brings forth green growth, grain, gardens, and fruits; it develops the productive plant side from which dry flood debris later comes.

terra: The Quranic ٱلْحَوَايَا means entrails in a dietary ruling; the source section explicitly uses the same dictionary form for winding hollows filled by floodwater, so the bodily sense exposes the shared coiled shape.

luna: The section traces cloud water into valleys and pasture; this ayah drives heavy clouds to a dead land, sends rain, and brings out fruits. Its context makes rain's productive result a sign of mercy. | terra: Winds carry heavy clouds to dead land, where rain produces every fruit; the scene links gathered cloud water to useful revival.

luna: This follows 7:57's rain: good land yields its plants by its Lord's permission, while bad land yields little. It gives a concrete image of different receptivity to what is provided, like the section's beneficial reminder. | terra: The good land yields plants by its Lord's leave while bad land yields only scantily, showing that the same water does not become retained benefit in every receiver.
terra: The flood saves Noah and those with him in the ark while drowning the deniers, distinguishing what overwhelming water preserves from what it removes.

luna: The section's خَلِيقَة is a hollow in rock where water gathers; here twelve springs gush from the rock and each group عَلِمَ its drinking place. The springs emerge rather than collect, but the ayah supplies a close rock-and-water counterpart and the named علم family. | terra: The rock sends out twelve springs and every tribe عَلِمَ its drinking place, again bringing the section's rock cavity, abundant water, and the root of “knows” into one scene.
terra: God establishes truth and nullifies falsehood, expressing the same separation that 13:17 depicts as water or useful metal beneath passing foam.

luna: The section's ج ه ر dictionary entry describes clearing mud until well water emerges; this ayah sends down water to purify people. The cleansing differs in object, but makes water's removal of impurity an explicit Quranic function.
terra: This ayah names gold and silver hoarded instead of spent for good, identifying the metal whose heating in 9:35 turns the useful-or-ornamental metal scene into a judgment on withheld benefit.

terra: The gold and silver named in 9:34 are heated in hellfire and used to brand their hoarders; this reverses 13:17's fire-worked metal for ornament or useful goods into hoarded metal that becomes punishment.

luna: The section's pasture turns to debris; here rain makes the earth's growth lush, then it is harvested as though it had not flourished the day before. The abrupt loss sharpens the difference between a season's display and what remains. | terra: The parable of worldly life begins with heavenly water and luxuriant growth, then leaves the land harvested as though it had not flourished, emphasizing passing appearance.
terra: An admonition from the Lord is called healing, guidance, and mercy, specifying the kinds of good that a beneficial reminder helps its hearer reach.
terra: Noah and his companions are saved in the ark and made successors while the rejecters are drowned, another explicit preservation/removal boundary within one flood.
terra: God establishes truth by His words despite the criminals' dislike, corresponding to the enduring truth beneath 13:17's passing foam.

luna: The section describes a flood and what its current carries away; after Noah's flood, the earth is told to swallow its water and the sky to stop. This is the flood's recession, a counterpart to the section's gathering and flow. | terra: Earth is commanded to swallow its water, heaven to cease, and the floodwater subsides; the verse stages where overwhelming water goes and how it is withdrawn.
terra: بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ makes a God-given lawful remainder better than gain taken by fraud, a social form of beneficial residue.
terra: The brothers propose casting Joseph into غَيَابَتِ ٱلْجُبِّ, the well's hidden depth; this supplies the concealed-well object behind the source's act of clearing until water appears.
terra: Where 12:10 proposes the hidden depth of the well and 12:19 later lowers the bucket, this ayah contributes the actual placing of Joseph in that concealed hollow.
terra: With 12:10 identifying the well, this ayah contributes the water-drawer and lowered bucket; what the well reveals is Joseph, an apt reversal of uncovering hidden water.

luna: The section's ج ه ر dictionary form describes cleaning a well until water appears; this ayah contrasts hidden speech with speech declared جَهَرَ. The sense is different, but the same named root frames what is concealed and what becomes manifest. | terra: Within the approach to 13:17, hidden speech and one who جَهَرَ بِهِ are equally known; the ayah supplies the open/hidden root relation used by the section's well-clearing sense.

terra: In the approach to 13:17, one who calls false gods is like a person stretching hands toward water that never reaches the mouth; it is the section's beneficial water rendered present yet unreceived.

terra: Immediately before the flood parable, this ayah identifies رَبُّ ٱلسَّمَاوَاتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ as God; it lets the source's r-b-b family image of gathered abundant water meet 13:17's sender of rain.

luna: The section joins flood foam, measured valley flow, and useful metal scum in one image: the ayah says the valleys flow بِقَدَرِهَا, then زَبَدٌ goes while what benefits people remains. It gives the section's exact contrast between passing residue and enduring benefit. | terra: This is the section's controlling parallel: rain fills valleys بِقَدَرِهَا, the flood carries زَبَدًا, metalworking raises like foam, and what benefits people يَمْكُثُ while the foam goes away.

luna: After 13:17's foam-and-water parable, this ayah distinguishes those who answer their Lord from those who refuse and face a bad return. It supplies the response-side application of the section's reminder that benefits when it takes hold. | terra: Directly after the flood parable, this ayah distinguishes those who answer their Lord from those who do not; it applies the useful-versus-lost distinction to reception.

luna: After 13:17's foam-and-water parable and 13:18's response contrast, this ayah distinguishes recognizing the revealed truth from blindness and says only people of understanding remember. It continues the section's question of whether a reminder takes hold. | terra: Immediately after the flood parable and its application in 13:18, this ayah contrasts one who يَعْلَمُ that the revelation is truth with the blind and says only people of understanding remember; it joins knowledge, truth, and receptive remembrance.

luna: The section's proverb makes غُثَاء what goes away without value; this ayah compares the deeds of disbelievers to ashes blown by a storm wind. Both images make apparent effort unable to remain or yield. | terra: The deeds of disbelievers are ashes violently scattered by wind and cannot be retained, paralleling the section's disregarded plant refuse that goes away.

luna: The section's reminder is valuable if it benefits and its water image rests on growth; this ayah likens a good word to a good tree with a firm root and high branches. It makes the word's benefit look rooted and growing. | terra: A good word is a good tree whose root is ثابت, giving the section's beneficial remainder a stable vegetal counterpart.

luna: This continues 14:24's good-tree comparison: the tree yields fruit continually by its Lord's permission, and God gives the comparison so people may remember. It joins lasting yield to a reminder that takes root. | terra: The stable tree of 14:24 continually gives fruit by its Lord's permission; this ayah contributes the lasting thing's recurring benefit.

luna: The section contrasts useful water with waste that leaves; this ayah likens a bad word to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability. It supplies the opposite of the good, rooted yield. | terra: The corrupt word is a bad tree uprooted from the earth with no قرار, the vegetal opposite of both held water and what remains in the ground.

luna: The section says the Hereafter is more abiding; this ayah says God makes believers firm in worldly life and the Hereafter. It extends the tree's stability into the two lives named by the section.
terra: Water sent from heaven brings fruits as provision and stands beside subjected rivers, another compact sequence from rain to enduring human benefit.
terra: The prayer addresses رَبَّنَا as knowing what people hide and disclose, combining the Lord root with the same concealed/revealed knowledge behind the clear-water image.

luna: The section links 13:17's valley flow by measure to the root of 87:3; this ayah says what is sent down is only by a known measure. It places the measured water scene within God's measured provision. | terra: All things have divine خزائن and descend only بِقَدَرٍ مَعْلُومٍ; this states the hidden provision and measured release presupposed by the section's retained water.

terra: After 15:21's measured storehouses, this ayah sends fertilizing winds, gives water to drink, and says humans are not its keepers; its own contribution is the water and the limit on human storage.

luna: The section sets flood-borne pasture against water held in hollows; this ayah says rain provides drink and vegetation where livestock graze. It supplies the useful, living side of the same water-and-pasture scene. | terra: Heavenly water provides both drink and vegetation in which livestock graze, joining useful water to pasture before it can become dry refuse.
luna: The section connects cloud water with pasture and benefit; this ayah says water grows crops, olives, dates, grapes, and fruit. It names the produce that makes water beneficial.
terra: Water sent from heaven revives dead earth and is called a sign for people who listen, linking water's benefit to receptive hearing.

luna: The section defines ب ق ي as remaining in one's first state and opposes it to perishing; this ayah says what you have runs out while what is with God remains. It gives the exact passing-and-remaining distinction behind the image. | terra: مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍ states in bare terms the section's division between what runs out and what remains.

luna: The section's cleaned-well sense is water emerging after mud is removed, and 13:17 separates foam from what benefits; this ayah says truth comes and falsehood vanishes. It gives the same clear separation in moral terms. | terra: Truth arrives and falsehood is زَهُوقًا, destined to vanish; it states directly what 13:17 makes visible through disappearing foam.
terra: The Quran is healing and mercy for believers but increases wrongdoers only in loss, clarifying 87:9's condition that a reminder must actually benefit its receiver.
terra: Earth's adornment is destined to become barren ground, a non-water version of luxuriant surface growth ending as lifeless residue.

luna: The section traces water into pasture and then debris; this ayah introduces a man with two grape gardens, date palms, and crops between them. It gives a garden-and-crop setting for the later question of what endures.

luna: The section describes water gathering and supporting growth; this ayah says both gardens yielded fruit and a river flowed through them. It is a specific picture of water retained among productive plants.

luna: The section says worldly growth passes and the Hereafter is more abiding; this garden owner boasts that he does not think his garden will ever perish. His claim is the direct false boundary the section's permanence distinction corrects.

luna: The section says the Hereafter is better and more abiding; this owner doubts the Hour and imagines an even better return if he is brought back to his Lord. It shows how confidence in present abundance can displace the section's lasting measure.

luna: Before 18:41's warning that the garden's water may sink, this ayah says the Lord may give a better garden or make the present one a slippery plain. It supplies the neighboring threat of losing the productive landscape.

luna: The section's hollows and wells hold water until it appears clear; this garden owner's water may instead become غَوْرًا, beyond his reach. That is the image's direct boundary: stored water can disappear below the ground. | terra: Garden water may become غَوْرًا, sunk beyond recovery; it supplies the explicit opposite of water lodged accessibly in earth or a rock hollow.

luna: After 18:41's water may become unreachable, this ayah reports the garden's fruit surrounded and its owner wringing his hands. It gives the actual loss that the preceding water warning completes.

luna: The section reads غُثَاء as dried vegetation floating on a flood; this ayah makes rain-grown vegetation هَشِيمًا scattered by winds. Its own context supplies a close image of provision's brief green stage ending in dispersed plant matter. | terra: The worldly-life parable begins with rain and mixed vegetation and ends as هَشِيمًا scattered by winds, a direct nonlexical counterpart to useful water outlasting disregarded dry growth.

luna: After 18:45's rain-grown plants are scattered by wind, this ayah calls wealth and children worldly adornment and says abiding good deeds are better. It makes the section's passing pasture and lasting benefit explicit in the next ayah. | terra: Worldly wealth and children are adornment, while ٱلْبَاقِيَاتُ ٱلصَّالِحَاتُ are better with the Lord; it names the morally valuable remainder behind the water image.

terra: On the reading reflected by حَمِئَةٍ, the sun is found setting at a muddy spring; that mud-and-water conjunction recalls the source's well whose water is obscured by mud, though the ayah is not about cleaning it.

luna: The section mentions foam produced when metal is melted for useful things; this ayah heats iron and pours molten copper into a barrier. It is a secondary metalworking parallel, though it says nothing about foam. | terra: Iron is heated until it is firelike and molten copper is poured over it, directly restaging the metal-and-fire half of the foam parable.
terra: Even a sea used as ink would run out before the words of رَبِّى run out; finite water is reversed into a measure of the inexhaustible divine word.

luna: The section connects benefit to good and names the Hereafter as more abiding; this ayah says enduring good deeds are better in reward and return. It identifies what can remain as a useful deed. | terra: After guidance increases, ٱلْبَاقِيَاتُ ٱلصَّالِحَاتُ are declared better in reward and return, linking reception of guidance to what endures.
terra: The revelation is specifically تَذْكِرَةً لِّمَن يَخْشَىٰ, the same reminder-and-fear relation that makes the section's offered water useful rather than lost.
terra: تَجْهَرْ is set against السِّرَّ وَأَخْفَىٰ under God's knowledge, almost reproducing 87:7 while the source section opens j-h-r into the image of clearing mud until water appears.

luna: The section links rainwater and pasture; this ayah says God made the earth a cradle, sent rain from the sky, and brought out varied plants. It gives the land-and-water setting in which pasture becomes provision. | terra: Water from heaven brings forth diverse pairs of plants, the growth stage presupposed by the section's dry vegetation and flood-borne debris.

luna: This follows the rain-grown plants in 20:53 and tells people to eat and graze their livestock. It makes explicit the useful yield of vegetation, the stage before the section's pasture turns to refuse. | terra: After 20:53's rain-grown plants, people are told to eat and pasture their cattle; this ayah contributes the vegetation's human and animal benefit.
terra: The magicians reject Pharaoh's coercion with وَٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, making “better and more lasting” an enacted choice rather than an abstraction.

luna: The section calls the Hereafter better and more abiding than the lower life; this ayah says not to covet worldly adornment because the Lord's provision is better and more enduring. It restates the section's measure of what lasts. | terra: The fading زَهْرَةَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا is set against the Lord's provision as خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, joining vegetation, divine provision, goodness, and permanence.
terra: A destroyed people persist in their cry until they are made حَصِيدًا خَامِدِينَ, harvested and extinguished; it parallels people reduced to the dry refuse represented by غُثَاء.

luna: The section's foam is discarded while the beneficial remains; this ayah says truth is cast against falsehood until falsehood vanishes. It sharpens the image's separation into a truth-and-falsehood boundary. | terra: Truth is cast against falsehood until it crushes it and falsehood is زَاهِقٌ, another direct verbal statement of the foam parable's moral action.
terra: Every living thing is made from water, stating the most basic reason water is the beneficial element beneath the passing surface debris.
terra: God knows ٱلْجَهْرَ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْلِ and what people conceal, directly pairing the source section's j-h-r root with knowing the hidden.

luna: The section moves from water and drying pasture to the Hereafter; this ayah says rain makes dead earth stir and grow, using that visible change as evidence for resurrection. It links the land's renewal to the afterlife claim.
terra: A بِئْرٍ مُّعَطَّلَةٍ is an abandoned well amid ruined settlements, the direct opposite of the source dictionary's water-rich well.
terra: Rain makes the earth become green, a concise instance of water producing the living surface later contrasted with dried refuse.

luna: The section's rock hollows gather cloud water and 13:17 measures valley flow; here water is sent down بِقَدَرٍ, settled in the earth, and can be taken away. It makes both measured storage and its limit explicit. | terra: Water descends from heaven بِقَدَرٍ, is lodged in the earth, and can be taken away; it joins the section's measure, retained water, and possibility of loss in one scene.

luna: The source section identifies غُثَاء as both flood-borne plants and a proverb for what disappears without value; this ayah says a punished people were made غُثَاءً. The word transfers the image of scattered refuse to a vanished community. | terra: The blast makes the destroyed people غُثَاءً; the exact word used for 87:5 here bears its flood-scum sense, turning the disregarded floating refuse into a fate.
terra: A thirsty person takes a mirage for water and finds nothing there, the perceptual opposite of the section's real, useful water that remains.
terra: Clouds are driven, joined, and heaped before rain emerges from them, detailing how the cloud water named by the source dictionary gathers and is released.
terra: God خَلَقَ everything and فَقَدَّرَهُ تَقْدِيرًا; the same creation-measure sequence underlies the capacities of the section's valleys and hollows.

luna: The section says غُثَاء can stand for what vanishes and is not counted; this ayah turns deeds into scattered dust. It gives a second Quranic image for value that leaves no durable remainder. | terra: Rejected deeds become هَبَاءً مَّنثُورًا, scattered dust; this is another concrete Quranic image for what is dispersed and not counted as benefit.

luna: The section's well is cleaned until its water appears clear; this ayah calls rainwater طَهُورًا. It gives a Quranic image of water as purifying, while the section's dictionary sense focuses on clearing a well. | terra: God sends مَاءً طَهُورًا from heaven; its purity directly answers the source dictionary's well cleared until the water appears and becomes clear.

luna: The section's gathered water supports what benefits; this ayah says rain revives a dead land and gives drink to people and livestock. It shows the useful yield of water from the sky. | terra: The pure water of 25:48 revives dead land and gives drink to cattle and people; this ayah contributes the water's concrete benefit.
terra: Moses reaches Midian's watering place and finds a crowd watering livestock while two women hold back, a concrete scene around an abundant shared water source.
terra: After 28:23 identifies the watering place and need, Moses waters the women's flock; this ayah contributes water becoming an immediate act of benefit.

luna: The section contrasts fading debris with the Hereafter, خير and أبقى; this ayah calls worldly life enjoyment and adornment, then says what is with God is better and more lasting. It states the same value boundary. | terra: Worldly goods are temporary enjoyment and adornment, while what is with God is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, exactly the section's better-and-lasting axis.

luna: After 28:60 says what is with God is better and more enduring than worldly enjoyment, this ayah asks whether the person promised good will be like one given only worldly enjoyment. It carries the section's passing-versus-lasting distinction into accountability.

luna: The section's account of what vanishes and what abides meets this ayah's claim that everything perishes except God's face. It gives the sharpest general boundary between passing creation and what remains. | terra: كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ draws the ultimate boundary between perishing things and the one abiding reality.
terra: Worldly life is play and diversion while the hereafter is the true life, sharpening the section's distinction between passing appearance and enduring reality.

luna: The section follows cloud water into valleys and grass; this ayah describes winds driving clouds until rain emerges. It adds the cloud's movement as a direct water-source scene. | terra: Winds raise clouds, God spreads and fragments them, and rain emerges from within; this repeats in detail the collection and release of the cloud-water named by the source.
luna: This ayah adds that before the rain described in 30:48, people had been in despair. It makes the arrival of gathered water a specific reversal from lack to provision.
luna: This follows 30:48–49's rain and says to look at how God revives the earth after its death. It connects water's growth to the section's lasting-life contrast.
terra: Even a mustard-seed hidden inside a صَخْرَةٍ is known and brought forth by God, joining the section's rock cavity to its theme of what is hidden yet known.
terra: A sea replenished by seven more seas still cannot exhaust God's words, giving the passing-water/enduring-word relation an even larger formulation.
terra: Water is driven to barren land and brings crops eaten by livestock and people, linking conveyed water, pasture, and concrete benefit.
terra: Iron is made pliable for David, supplying the worked-metal action that stands beside floodwater in 13:17's paired foam image.
terra: David is told to make armor and قَدِّرْ فِى ٱلسَّرْدِ, bringing useful metalwork and exact measure together as 13:17 does.
terra: A spring of molten copper is made to flow for Solomon, combining liquid movement with the melted metal of 13:17's second comparison.
terra: قُدُورٍ رَّاسِيَاتٍ names fixed cauldrons, the exact vessel behind the source dictionary's secondary phrase “foam of the flood and of the cooking pot,” though this ayah mentions no foam.

luna: This precedes 34:16's flood: it describes Sheba's two gardens and tells them to eat their Lord's provision. That prior fertility makes the next ayah's flood-driven loss a specific reversal of useful growth.

luna: The section names hollows filled by a torrent; this ayah names the flood of the dam, which replaces Sheba's fruitful gardens with scant, bitter growth. It shows a flood removing the landscape's useful abundance.
terra: Truth comes and falsehood can neither originate nor restore anything, a further verbal counterpart to the foam parable's vanishing falsehood.

luna: The section traces cloud water to pasture; this ayah says winds drive clouds and God uses them to revive dead land. It is another direct formulation of wind, cloud, and renewed growth. | terra: Winds raise clouds that are driven to dead land and revive it, a repeated formulation of gathered cloud-water becoming useful life.

terra: One body of water is fresh and pleasant to drink while another is salty and bitter, yet both yield food and adornment; the verse distinguishes kinds of water and kinds of benefit rather than treating all water alike.
terra: Warning benefits the one who follows the reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, closely repeating 87:9–10's reminder-and-fear condition.
terra: Dead earth is revived and yields grain for eating; it supplies the revival stage immediately before the gardens and springs of 36:34–35.
terra: Gardens are given springs flowing through them, a cultivated counterpart to water gathering and remaining in the earth.
terra: The springs and gardens of 36:34 yield fruit for people to eat and invite gratitude; this ayah contributes the retained water's benefit.
terra: Livestock provide مَنَافِعُ وَمَشَارِبُ, putting the benefit root beside things drunk and thereby echoing useful water as provision.
terra: Paradisal provision is described as having no depletion, a direct formulation of beneficial provision that remains instead of running out.

luna: The section's pasture becomes floating dry growth; here rain enters streams in the earth and the crop yellows before Allah makes it حُطَامًا. This repeats the whole growth-to-debris movement beside the water source. | terra: God sends down water, conducts it as springs within the earth, then the plants yellow and become حُطَامًا; stored water and passing plant refuse form the section's two faces here.
terra: Worldly life is temporary enjoyment while the hereafter is دَارُ ٱلْقَرَارِ, the abode of settled permanence rather than passing surface matter.
terra: A lifeless, humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends, making the water's life-giving benefit visible.
terra: The revelation is guidance and healing for believers but deafness and blindness for others, another precise boundary between water-like benefit and failed reception.
terra: God erases falsehood and confirms truth by His words, a conceptual rendering of the foam being removed while what has value remains.
terra: Provision is sent down بِقَدَرٍ because unrestricted plenty would corrupt, giving the section's measured provision a stated moral reason.

luna: The section says the Hereafter is better and more abiding; this ayah names worldly provision as enjoyment and what is with God as better and more enduring. It turns the image's passing-versus-staying distinction into a judgment about provision. | terra: Worldly possessions are merely temporary enjoyment, but what is with God is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ for believers who trust their Lord.

luna: The section explicitly links 13:17's بِقَدَرِهَا to the root of 87:3; here water is sent بِقَدَرٍ and revives a dead land. It joins measured rain to growth rather than to flood residue. | terra: Water comes from heaven بِقَدَرٍ and revives a dead land, a direct meeting of measured water, useful growth, and return from lifelessness.
terra: The condemned are told إِنَّكُم مَّاكِثُونَ, using the same staying root as 13:17 to show that permanence itself is not identical with benefit.
terra: Paradise contains rivers of مَاءٍ غَيْرِ آسِنٍ, water whose state does not alter; it literalizes the source definition of permanence as remaining in an original condition.

luna: The section follows rain into useful pasture; this ayah describes blessed water from the sky bringing gardens and grain. It names another Quranic rain-fed growth scene. | terra: Blessed water descends from heaven and grows gardens and harvested grain, a compact instance of water becoming lasting provision.
luna: This continues 50:9's blessed rain and names tall palms with clustered fruit. It makes the yield of the water scene specific.

luna: This closes 50:9–10's rain-and-crop scene by calling its yield provision for servants and a revival of dead land. It connects water's benefit to renewal. | terra: The growth from 50:9 is provision for servants and revives a dead land, stating both benefit and life-giving persistence.
terra: A reminder exists for one who has a heart or listens attentively; the receptive hearer supplies the human analogue to a hollow that holds useful water.
terra: The Prophet is told to remind with the Quran the one who fears the warning, matching 87:9–10's command and its receptive, fearing hearer.
terra: The command وَذَكِّرْ is justified because remembrance تَنفَعُ believers, directly completing 87:9's conditional link between reminder and benefit.

luna: The section develops floodwater and cloud water; this ayah describes the sky opening with pouring water in Noah's flood. It supplies a direct Quranic flood scene. | terra: Heaven's gates open with pouring water, supplying the descending half of the flood scene that 54:12 completes when earth's springs meet it.

luna: The section describes flood-filled hollows and water gathering; this ayah says the earth burst with springs and the waters met. It adds the earth-side source to the flood's rain. | terra: Earth bursts into springs and the waters meet for an affair already قُدِرَ; gathered floodwater and measure coincide as they do in the section.
terra: The destroyed people become كَهَشِيمِ ٱلْمُحْتَظِرِ, dry broken plant matter, a close nonlexical counterpart to غُثَاء as the disregarded remainder of destruction.
terra: إِنَّا كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَاهُ بِقَدَرٍ joins creation and measure exactly as 87:2–3 do, while nearby 54:11–12 embody that measure in floodwater.

luna: The section contrasts fleeting surface waste with what remains; this ayah says everyone on earth is perishing. It states the boundary of created permanence that the section's image implies. | terra: كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ gives the vanishing side of the section's distinction at the scale of all earthly life.

luna: The section defines abiding as the opposite of perishing; this ayah says the face of the Lord remains. It gives the enduring side of the boundary stated in 55:26. | terra: After 55:26 says all earthly life passes, this ayah contributes the abiding وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ, the enduring side of the pair.

luna: The section's pasture may become floating waste; this ayah says God could make the crop حُطَامًا after people sow it. The possibility of losing the harvest makes the useful growth in the section contingent rather than permanent.
terra: The question أَفَرَءَيْتُمُ ٱلْمَاءَ ٱلَّذِى تَشْرَبُونَ directs attention to water precisely as a received benefit.
terra: Humans do not send the water down from ٱلْمُزْنِ, the rain clouds; this supplies the cloud source of the water held in the section's rock hollows.
terra: God could make cloud-water أُجَاجًا, bitter; this marks the boundary between mere remaining liquid and the beneficial water the section values.

luna: The section's green pasture ends as غُثَاء; this ayah likewise moves from rain-grown plants to yellowing and حُطَامًا, then applies that cycle to worldly life. It directly joins the section's vegetation image to its claim that the Hereafter is more abiding. | terra: Rain-grown vegetation pleases, then yellows and becomes حُطَامًا while worldly life is deceptive enjoyment; it closely restages growth turning into disregarded debris.

luna: The section's 13:17 passage describes metal melted for useful objects and uses مَا يَنفَعُ النَّاسَ for what remains; this ayah names iron and its مَنَافِعُ لِلنَّاسِ. It connects the section's metal image to metal's concrete benefit. | terra: Iron is sent with great force and مَنَافِعُ لِلنَّاسِ; this joins 13:17's worked metal for useful objects to the section's root of benefit.
terra: Whether speech is concealed or made public with ٱجْهَرُوا, God knows what breasts contain; disclosure and hidden knowledge again form the well-clearing analogy's conceptual frame.
terra: Following 67:13's concealed and public speech, this ayah asks whether the One who خَلَقَ would not know, joining the section's creation and knowledge roots around hiddenness.

luna: The section follows water gathered in rock hollows and wells; this ayah asks who could bring flowing water if it became غَوْرًا. It turns the section's available, retained water into a stated dependence on God. | terra: If water sinks away, no one can bring مَاءٍ مَّعِينٍ; accessible flowing water is set against hidden, irretrievable water.
terra: Where 13:17's flood carries disregarded foam, overflowing water here carries and preserves the ancestors in the ark; the shared carrying action marks what the water discards versus saves.
terra: Following the overflowing water and rescue of 69:11, the event is made a تَذْكِرَةً retained by an attentive ear; this ayah contributes the explicit meeting of flood and held reminder.
terra: Noah says he called his people جِهَارًا, bringing the section's j-h-r root into a prophetic reminder whose failed reception eventually turns rainwater into a destroying flood.
terra: After Noah's open call in 71:8, this ayah contributes his combined public proclamation and secret appeal, a sustained open/hidden preaching stance close to 87:7–10.

luna: The section's root note describes abundant water as water gathered; this ayah promises rain مِّدْرَارًا. It gives an image of abundance from the sky that fills the section's water side. | terra: As the promised response to accepting Noah's reminder, heaven would send abundant rain; useful descending water is thus set inside the same surah as the later flood of rejection.

luna: This follows 71:11's abundant rain and names gardens and rivers among God's provisions. It completes the rain-to-stored-water-to-useful-growth relation developed in the section. | terra: Following 71:11's abundant rain, this ayah contributes gardens and rivers among the resulting provisions, making the water's retained benefit explicit.
terra: After Noah's public and secret calls and the offered rain of 71:8–12, the rejecters are drowned for their sins; water changes from promised provision to judgment when reminder is refused.
terra: Steadfastness on the way is answered with مَاءً غَدَقًا, abundant water; the moral condition and plentiful provision meet the section's water-rich lexical senses.

luna: The section's dictionary entries center water gathering among rocks and hollows; this ayah pairs high mountains with sweet water given to drink. It is a close mountain-and-water provision image. | terra: Lofty mountains are placed on earth and people are given sweet water to drink, bringing rock, gathered fresh water, and provision into one ayah.

luna: The section describes water carried from clouds into valleys; this ayah says rain is poured down from clouds. It supplies the cloud-to-ground part of a rain-fed plant sequence. | terra: Pouring water descends from the rain clouds, a direct formulation of the cloud-water that the source's rock hollows receive.

luna: After 78:14's pouring rain, this ayah names grain and vegetation growing from it. It gives the useful growth stage before the section's pasture becomes refuse. | terra: After 78:14's pouring rain, this ayah contributes grain and vegetation brought out by it, showing the water becoming useful growth.

luna: This continues 78:14–15's rain and vegetation with dense gardens. It makes the productive landscape created by water explicit. | terra: This completes 78:14–15 with dense gardens, the lasting cultivated result of descending water.
terra: Earth brings forth مَاءَهَا وَمَرْعَىٰهَا, placing water and pasture side by side as the section's flood, held rain, and dry herbage require.
terra: After 79:31 names earth's water and pasture, this ayah identifies them as provision for people and livestock, stating why the retained water matters.
terra: The Prophet is only a warner to the one who fears the Hour, repeating the section's stance that admonition reaches its intended effect in a fearing hearer.
terra: Immediately before 80:4 says reminder may benefit him, this ayah contributes the possibility that the neglected hearer may purify himself.
terra: The overlooked man may remember فَتَنفَعَهُ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ; this gives a human scene for the section's image of a reminder becoming retained benefit.

luna: The section traces useful water to clouds and valleys; this ayah says God pours water abundantly as the beginning of the food sequence in 80:25–32. It gives the rain that makes the land productive. | terra: أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَاءَ صَبًّا presents the forceful pouring of water that begins the section's movement from rain to channels and growth.

luna: The section's rain gathers in rock hollows and feeds pasture; this ayah says the earth is split open in the same food sequence. It supplies the earth's opening for growth. | terra: Earth is split open after the poured water of 80:25, showing the receiving ground through which useful growth emerges.
luna: The section's water sustains vegetation before it dries into refuse; this ayah names grain among the growth produced after rain and split earth. It marks the useful crop stage.
luna: The section's water sustains vegetation; this ayah adds grapes and foddering greens to the food sequence begun by rain. These are concrete yields of the water that the section follows.
luna: The section's water sustains vegetation; this ayah names olives and palms among the crops in the rain-fed sequence. It makes the growth's material benefit specific.
luna: The section's water sustains vegetation; this ayah adds dense gardens to the same sequence of crops. The gardens are the productive landscape before the section's image turns to debris.

luna: The section follows water into useful plant growth; this ayah names fruit and أَبًّا, fodder, among the outputs of rain and split earth. The latter is especially close to pasture for grazing. | terra: Fruit and أَبًّا, herbage or pasture, are among the products of the poured water, linking rain directly to the plant matter later left dry.

luna: At the end of the food sequence begun with water in 80:25, this ayah calls the produce provision for people and livestock. It makes explicit the benefit of the growth the section follows. | terra: The rain-grown foods of 80:27–31 are called provision for people and livestock, making explicit the benefit side of the image.
terra: فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنتَ مُذَكِّرٌ repeats the prophetic stance of offering reminder whose reception determines whether it benefits.
terra: The later state is declared better than the former, echoing both the section's خَيْرٌ judgment and the “first” language embedded in its definition of permanence.
terra: The army is made like عَصْفٍ مَّأْكُولٍ, consumed straw, another Quranic transformation of the rejected into worthless plant debris.
